title: Equal Balance of Samādhi and Prajñā for the Buddha-Reciter
author: Zhanran
excerpt: Question: I have already achieved thought-after-thought continuity. What is the next step in practice?

inline.s: Rest in the Buddha-name; give rise to no discriminating thought —
Hold samādhi and prajñā in equal balance; keep constant watch by day and night.
Prajñā: all appearances whatsoever are false and illusory.
Samādhi: grasp at no appearance
abide unmoved, as such.
Samādhi and prajñā held in equal balance.
Question: I have already achieved thought-after-thought continuity. What is the next step in practice?

Answer: Congratulations on achieving thought-after-thought continuity. At this point you should understand the truth of the first principle, so as to seek rebirth in the highest grade. To this end I suggest you read
Mind, Self-nature, and Tathāgatagarbha
and
The True Appearance of All Dharmas
. Your next step in practice is:
rest in the Buddha-name, give rise to no discrimination, hold samādhi and prajñā in equal balance, and keep constant watch by day and night.
This is the very practice of Buddha-recitation samādhi. It is explained below:
To settle the mind upon the Buddha-name is what Master Shandao taught:
“Let the recitation continue thought after thought, taking your whole life as its term.
Walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, you must spur your mind and subdue yourself, never letting it lapse by day or night.”
(See
Master Shandao's Pure Land Teachings
for details.)

[Spur the mind, subdue oneself] To urge oneself on and to restrain oneself. These four words — “spur the mind, subdue oneself” — are a mighty weapon for overcoming difficulty and sweeping away obstacles. “Subdue oneself”: to restrain oneself. [Never lapse by day or night] Never, by day or by night, allow the thought-after-thought continuity to cease.

Turn the mind that broods over worldly affairs (this creates the karma of saṃsāra) back to the Buddha-name (this cultivates pure karma). The moment the mind wanders off and broods over worldly affairs, return it at once to the Buddha-name. Keep up the work of “gathering it back the instant it slips away,” until the mind can rest steadily upon the Buddha-name.
[Cultivate pure karma] When pure karma is brought to completion, one can know beforehand the time of one's death.

Discrimination means weighing and distinguishing among the features of things — self and other, right and wrong, good and evil, fair and foul, beautiful and ugly — and thereby giving rise to a mind of liking and disliking, grasping and rejecting. Thus one is turned by circumstances and revolves through birth and death. The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra,
Fascicle Five Hundred and Seventy-six, says:

“Although all these dharmas are like illusions, sentient beings, deluded and uncomprehending, take what is not to be what is, and take the impermanent to be permanent. Amid the dharmas they make all manner of discriminations — now discriminating form, now discriminating mind; the conditioned and the unconditioned, the defiled and the undefiled — discriminations of every sort. Because of these discriminations they do not know, in truth, that all dharmas are like illusions; and because they do not know, they revolve through birth and death
(because they do not know in truth that all dharmas are like illusions, they revolve through birth and death)
Discrimination arises from the deluded mind; the true mind sees all things as alike. The Fourth Patriarch of the Chan school, Daoxin, said:

“Circumstances have no good or bad in themselves; good and bad arise from the mind. If the mind does not force names upon them, from what would deluded feelings arise? When deluded feelings no longer arise, the true mind extends its knowing everywhere. Simply be free wherever your mind goes; there is nothing more to be countered. This is called the ever-abiding dharmakāya, without change or alteration.”
(The Compendium of the Five Lamps)

[As such (ru)] The true, unchanging nature of all things. This nature is extremely hard to describe in words, so the single word “such” (ru) is borrowed to stand for it. The original nature is the true appearance of things, and the true appearance is “suchness”; because it is non-dual, unchanging, unmoving, and unaltered — the true face of all dharmas sharing one and the same appearance — it is called “such.”
Know that the mind is stirred by delusion, that there is no realm before you; practice the dharma of leaving, neither grasping nor dwelling.
[There is no realm before you] There is, in truth, no present realm, because it is an illusion. [Practice the dharma of leaving] Knowing an illusion is leaving it; leaving an illusion is awakening.
The way to give rise to no discriminative thought is:
contemplate the mind while reciting the Buddha-name.
That is to say:
at the very moment of reciting, contemplate the thought of that moment; if a deluded thought arises, know it and do not follow it.
(For the details of contemplating the mind while reciting, see the chapter “Contemplating the present thought” in
Aware Buddha-recitation
[Know it and do not follow it] The moment a deluded thought arises, return at once to the Buddha-name, and do not let the illusory delusion seize authority.
The essential point of the work is:
toward deluded thoughts, know them and do not follow them.

Not to know is to lack prajñā; to follow is to lack samādhi. To know and yet not follow is precisely samādhi and prajñā held in equal balance. Persist in this, and once the work deepens, discriminative thoughts cease of themselves. When discriminative thoughts no longer arise, where can the mark of self, the mark of a person, the mark of living beings, or the mark of a lifespan remain? To recite the Buddha-name free of all four marks is certain to bring rebirth in the highest grade.
[The four marks] The mark of self, the mark of a person, the mark of living beings, and the mark of a lifespan. (See
An In-depth Exposition of the Diamond Sūtra

blocks.text: Samādhi and prajñā held in equal balance

inline.s: To gather in the scattered mind is samādhi; to observe and illuminate the truth of all things is prajñā. The Diamond Sūtra says:
“All appearances whatsoever are false and illusory.”
“Grasping at no appearance, abiding unmoved, as such.”
Samādhi and prajñā held in equal balance means:
“grasping at no appearance, abiding unmoved, as such.”
To grasp at no appearance — to see through the illusory appearance — is prajñā. To abide unmoved, as such — to hold fast — is samādhi.
It is like a person in a dream who is chased by a fierce tiger, fleeing in terror and misery. Yet some people are able to
say to themselves at once: “This is a dream! This is a dream!” — and they awake. This is the wondrous method of saving oneself.

[The two truths] The conventional truth and the ultimate truth. The conventional truth is also called the worldly truth or the truth of mundane convention — the affairs and principles of the world as ordinary beings see them. The ultimate truth is also called the truth of the first principle or the supreme truth — the true, real principle seen by the wisdom of the sages

, that is, the true appearance of all dharmas. The true, real principle known and seen by the wisdom of the sages is free of all delusion, hence it is called “true”; its principle is eternally unchanging, hence it is called a “truth.” [The true appearance of all dharmas] “True appearance” means the real state of things; “the true appearance of all dharmas” means the real state of all things. The Buddha said:
“What is called the true appearance of all dharmas? It is that all dharmas are ultimately empty, with nothing to grasp.”
(The Buddha Treasury Sūtra)
For a detailed discussion of the true appearance of all dharmas, see
The True Appearance of All Dharmas

[Grasping at no appearance, abiding unmoved, as such] Do not cling to appearances as real or let yourself be moved by them. That is, do not attach to appearances, and do not stir the mind. [As such] The first “such” means “like”; the second “such” is true suchness (the original nature). “As such” means “like true suchness” — the state of non-moving, quiescent, equal, non-dual stillness, free of inverted discriminations.

Grasping at no appearance” — if, on meeting a circumstance (outer or inner), the mind is stirred and a feeling of love or hate, liking or disliking, arises, this is “grasping at appearances.” When the Buddha, on the eighth day of the twelfth month, looked upon the morning star and realized the Way, he said:
“How wondrous! All living beings are endowed with the wisdom and the marks of virtue of the Tathāgata. It is only because of deluded thoughts and attachments that they cannot realize them.”

And deluded thoughts and attachments all come from “grasping at appearances” (taking illusions to be real). Therefore, when meeting a circumstance, neither grasp nor dwell; examine yourself in every matter and at every place, and your work will fall on the vital point. The core of samādhi and prajñā held in equal balance is precisely leaving illusion:
grasping at no appearance, abiding unmoved, as such.
The Buddha said:
“Good man! Knowing an illusion, you leave it at once, with no expedient means; leaving an illusion, you are awakened, with no gradual stages.”
(The Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment)

The practice of “grasping at no appearance, abiding unmoved, as such” has two stages: subduing and letting be. To subdue is to achieve “grasping at no appearance, abiding unmoved, as such” by taming the mind. To let be is to achieve “grasping at no appearance, abiding unmoved, as such” naturally, without any forced suppression.

In the work of holding samādhi and prajñā in equal balance, you must, on the one hand, proceed step by step with feet planted firmly on the ground, while on the other hand, through understanding the principles and through repeated cultivation, you must turn around the deep-rooted view and thinking that takes illusions to be real. The courses of the “Prajñā shatters delusion” stage at the
Online Buddhist Academy of Practice as Taught

(An In-depth Exposition of the Diamond Sūtra, An In-depth Exposition of the Heart Sūtra, An In-depth Exposition of the Platform Sūtra of the Sixth Patriarch, Selected Annotations on the Buddha Treasury Sūtra, and An In-depth Exposition of the Straightforward Explanation of the True Mind) serve exactly this purpose. It is best to study these five courses systematically. If your work is busy and your time is pressing, you may first study carefully
An In-depth Exposition of the Heart Sūtra

blocks.text: Keeping constant watch by day and night

inline.s: To “keep watch” (tisi) is to maintain right mindfulness (the thought of Buddha-recitation) with vigilance. Master Lianchi said:
“May you set down the myriad entanglements and, through all twelve periods
(the twenty-four hours)
, keep watch thought after thought — this is my deepest wish.”
(The Yunqi Collection)
The Gateless Barrier of the Chan Tradition says:
“With all three hundred and sixty joints and eighty-four thousand pores of your whole body, raise up a single ball of doubt and investigate the word ‘wu’ (no), keeping watch by day and night.”
The Complete Works of Master Zhu, in the chapter “Nourishing the Mind,” says:
“Only keep constant watch over yourself, accumulate it bit by bit, and after a long time it will naturally continue on and merge into one seamless whole.”

Master Ruiyan asked himself every day: “Master, are you awake?” and answered himself: “Awake.” [Awake] Clear-minded and alert. For a practitioner, to fall into deluded thought or into dullness and torpor is to be unclear-minded, because one has not taken charge of oneself.
The truth stands clear within yourself — why ask abroad of rise or fall?
At every touch turn back the light, lest worldly toil the master thrall.

[The matter] This affair. [Within yourself] In your own person — what you yourself personally carry out. [Worldly toil] The mind laboring over the objects of the senses; another name for the afflictions. [The master] The master within — one's own true nature.
This verse is taken from
Master Hanshan Deqing
's Dream Wanderings Collection, from the “Ten Poems Left in Farewell to the Disciples of the Lingnan Dharma Society on Setting Out for the Southern Peak.”
